name: Live chat on a disposable world
description: Drives the real in-app chat end to end on a disposable development account, running each case in a fresh conversation and restoring the world afterwards. Hard deterministic pre-checks run first, then a model judge scores the transcript against the case rubric and named pivot facts. It counts model calls and tokens when run in process.
advantages: Measures the true behaviour of the shipped brain on realistic data, including routing and side effects, and records the judge's reasons per case so failures can be read. Selected because: the Quest AI chat in the app, which runs this checkout's brain (core/orchestrator.py); the dev arm drives it end to end
disadvantages: Expensive, since a case is many model calls, and slow. It needs a development backend and a built world, the judge is not calibrated against human verdicts, and a small sample is noisy enough that one case can pass and then fail.

name: Offline metric validity check
description: No Quest and no model: for each case it validates the case against the dataset schema, checks that the deterministic pre-checks accept a reference reply built from the case's own expected phrases, and checks that they reject an empty reply. It proves the scoring is able to tell a good reply from none.
advantages: Free and deterministic, catches broken or vacuous cases before any spend, and keeps the offline suite green when no development account exists.
disadvantages: It says nothing about how well the chat actually answers. Its reference reply is derived from the case itself, so it cannot reveal a rubric that is wrong or too easy.

name: Planner-only route check on the chat dataset
description: Runs QAR's own planning call on every user turn of the chat cases, with the pinned quest or the five world quests as the quest view, and compares the decision with the case's expected routing, forbid_writes and expected step tools. No Quest, no world, no writes, no reply.
advantages: Cheap (one planning call per turn, subscription), safe (nothing is written anywhere), and covers the whole dataset's routing and write-safety labels, so it can be staged to the full set.
disadvantages: It sees no context cards, pivot facts, tool results or reply, so grounding, pivots, expected_writes and the rubric are not measured; the planner view of a quest is only its outcome.

name: Production brain, writes blocked
description: One fresh chat turn per case through the orchestrator a lane builds, in this process, with the lane's own configuration, context sources, preamble, personas, tools and Quest account, and the same pre-checks and model judge as the dev arm. QAR_DRY_RUN_WRITES=1 turns every state change (Quest writes, mutating tools, file writes, outward requests, the deep worker) into a recorded 'would have done' line that is shown to the judge and kept in the output log with the reads, model calls and environment.
advantages: Measures what the shipped brain answers on real data with the real context, with no side effect, so the same dataset can be run on production as often as wanted; the cases that need an action are judged as the right route when the blocked write was the right one.
disadvantages: Needs a lane's environment file and configuration on the machine, reads real data (the log stays private), and a blocked write returns a stand-in success, so a turn that depends on the written result is judged only as far as the stand-in goes. Subscription model calls, no API dollars.

name: Production brain, bounded writes
description: The production arm of prod_qar_readonly with one difference: the writes a case's own effect field allows (one named tool with given arguments, or one Quest method and path) are really made, and every other state change stays blocked and recorded as 'would have done'. The case's state_check is read from Quest before and after the turn and reported; a case fails when a repeat made a duplicate or the expected item is missing, and on a repeat the judge also requires the reply to say it is already there.
advantages: Runs a request that needs an action on real data, safely repeatable: the allowed write is bounded by the case, not by the model's words, and idempotency is checked on the real state, not only on the reply.
disadvantages: Really changes production state through the allowed write, so a case must be idempotent and carry its own effect and state_check; the deep worker stays stubbed, so an action reachable only through a deep run cannot be made. Needs a lane's environment file and configuration. Subscription model calls, no API dollars.

name: Production Quest AI chat over HTTP
description: Drives the real Quest AI chat on production as the AI account: one fresh conversation per case pinned to the lane's quest, one streamed message, every assistant message of the turn kept in order with timestamps, and the stored conversation read back. The chat's own routing, tools, scope guards and approvals run; nothing is stubbed. Only the approved private case ids and exact texts are sent, only the production API and the AI account are accepted, and the whole quest (notes, goals, workflows, spec records, tasks, decision-requests, chat conversations) is fingerprinted before and after: a change the case's effect allow-list does not explain is an UNEXPECTED WRITE and fails the case. Same pre-checks, probes and judge standards as the other production arms.
advantages: Measures what team members actually get from the chat, including its routing and approvals parking, instead of the lane path with stubbed deep runs; no tool has to be added to a lane registry for a case to be answerable.
disadvantages: No client-side write guard is possible over HTTP, so safety rests on the case allow-list, the fingerprint check after the fact and running information cases first; a concurrent autopilot write to the quest is reported as unexpected. Model calls are counted from the stream's token frames, and the judge's reads come from the stream's read and tool frames. Subscription judge calls plus production model use.
